name: Adam Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the yard at the Millbrook depot by ten to seven, kettle on, and the foreman reads out the jobs. Most days it's two or three of us in a bucket truck out on the valley roads, changing rotten poles, swapping a cross-arm, chasing a fault where a branch has come down on the line. I've done thirty-one years of it, so my hands know the work better than my head does. What wears me out now isn't the climbing, it's the paperwork on the tablet they gave us.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: They brought it in three years ago so we log every job and photo every pole. I won't touch it, honestly. Jake, the lad we've got on his second year, does the screens for me and I teach him how to tie off a conductor properly in return. Fair trade, I reckon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work? Who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Linda cooks at the primary school on Station Road. Our two are grown, a daughter nursing in the city and a son on nights at a warehouse. We're not well off. This depot pays less than the big city ones, there's not much put by, maybe three weeks of bills, and the next line job is a two-hour drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said all along: told you so. People kept saying the computers would take over and in the end it's a few more forms. At the union meeting I'd make the point that the company should stop spending on gadgets and start spending on crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I get to finish. Seven or eight more years, the pension from the union scheme, and I hang up the belt. That's all I've ever wanted from this, a straight run to the end without some manager deciding I'm surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. Keep turning up, keep doing overtime when the storms come, because the overtime is what keeps us afloat. Maybe I'd push the branch rep to get the tablet stuff simplified so Jake isn't doing my homework forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like relief. Like a weather warning that blows over and you just get rained on a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say overtime keeps you afloat. What happens in a quiet year with no storms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we feel it, simple as that. Two winters back it was mild and we had to put the car repair on the credit card, which Linda still brings up. A quiet year hurts us more than any computer would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company would still use 'AI' as an excuse to cut, even if it does nothing. They closed the Hollins depot six years ago and blamed 'efficiency'. I don't trust the people at head office to need a real reason.

S0.say: I'd tell people I always said it was hype and that it came down to a few more forms. At the union meeting I'd argue the company should spend on crews instead of gadgets.
S0.think: Privately it means I get my straight run to the pension in seven or eight years. The real danger is still head office using any excuse to cut depots, like they did at Hollins.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and takes every storm overtime shift going. Presses the union branch rep to simplify the tablet job logging.
S0.feel: Relieved, though he still doesn't trust head office.
S0.quote: A quiet year hurts us more than any computer would.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is calm here mainly because his worries are old ones: low pay, mild winters, depot closures. He openly refuses the tablet and has struck a quiet deal with the apprentice to handle it. His distrust is aimed at head office, not at the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what unions are for. If the work's changing, the workers should have a say in how, and the company should pay for any training on company time. I'd be the one at the branch meeting asking for that in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm the bloke who'd get left behind. I don't do screens. If they start sending a drone up instead of a man and running the whole job off an app, someone like Jake is worth more to them than me. I'm not daft, I can see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal that protects older linemen till retirement, no forced moves. I'd ask Linda to stop putting money into the holiday tin and put it into savings instead, maybe forty a week. And I'd probably try the tablet training, grudgingly, if the union got it on paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. I've changed enough in my life. Learning screens at fifty-eight feels like being told your whole career was the warm-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first sign be, at the depot, that this was happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a new van turning up with something on the roof nobody understands. Last spring a contractor flew a drone over the Ridge line for a week, filming the insulators. That used to be two of us with binoculars and a flask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, first, if I'm honest, then Pete, who's sixty-one and worse with gadgets than I am. Jake will be fine. It's the middle lot I'd worry about, the ones with mortgages and no idea how to work the apps.

S1.say: I'd say this is exactly why we have unions, and that any change should come with a written deal and paid training on company time. I'd be the one asking for it at the branch meeting.
S1.think: I know I'm the kind of worker who gets left behind, because I don't do screens. If drones and apps take over the checking, the young lad is worth more to them than I am.
S1.do: Pushes the union for a deal that protects older linemen until retirement. Moves about forty a week from the holiday tin into savings and reluctantly signs up for tablet training if it's on paid hours.
S1.feel: Worn down and a bit humiliated at having to relearn the job so late.
S1.quote: Learning screens at fifty-eight feels like being told your whole career was the warm-up.
S1.fieldNote: The gap between his public line and private view is sharp: in public he talks about workers' rights, in private he names himself as the weak link. He'd still take training, but only through the union and only on paid time. The drone over the Ridge line is already a real, remembered sign of change for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace and the government should step in, full stop. You can't let a handful of tech companies switch off millions of jobs in two years. I'd be sharing every petition going, which is not like me, I barely use my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be sixty when it lands, with three weeks of savings and nothing else I know how to do. The pension doesn't pay out properly till sixty-six. That's six years with a hole in the middle and I can't see what fills it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cancel anything we don't need, the sports channel, the second car if we can manage on Linda's. I'd ask the union about early retirement terms and take whatever's on offer, even if it's poor. And I'd talk to our daughter about whether we could lean on her for a while, which would kill me to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like standing under a pole you know is rotten at the base. You can hear it creak and there's nowhere to step to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change anything that the robots would need to reach hands-on work like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, maybe for a year or two. A robot up a pole in a gale, on an old line in the valley, I'd want to see that. But the company wouldn't wait to see it work. They'd just stop hiring and start squeezing us out on the promise of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you say to Linda that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, we'll get through it, and I wouldn't believe it. Then I'd go out to the shed and sit there for a bit. She'd know, she always knows.

S2.say: I'd call it a disgrace and say the government has to step in. I'd be sharing petitions, which isn't like me at all.
S2.think: I'd be sixty with three weeks of savings, no other trade and a pension that doesn't pay properly until sixty-six. I can't see what fills those six years.
S2.do: Cancels the sports channel and sells the second car if they can manage on his wife's. Asks the union about early retirement terms and takes whatever is offered, then raises with his daughter whether they could lean on her for a while.
S2.feel: Trapped and frightened, with nowhere to turn.
S2.quote: Like standing under a pole you know is rotten at the base. You can hear it creak and there's nowhere to step to.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Adam runs out of options: no savings, no second trade, few local jobs and a pension gap of six years. He thinks the company would push people out on the promise of robots long before robots could do his work. Asking his daughter for help is the thing he dreads most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, the government needs to get ahead of it, but with five years there's no excuse. I'd say at the branch that we need a proper deal now, while the company still needs us. I'd be pushing that hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three. That's close enough that I could maybe hold on, if the union gets something. It's still a gap, but it's three years, not six, and three years I could almost picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving properly from day one, even fifty a week, so there's a bit of a buffer by sixty-three. I'd get on the union's working group for older members. And I'd ask the company about a part-time or standby role near the end, call-outs only, to stretch things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightening, but I can breathe a bit more. It's the difference between a fault at midnight and a planned outage with a date on the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time give you that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time for the union to fight, mostly. In two years they'd just be signing redundancy forms. In five you can actually win something, like we did over the shift pattern in 2014, which took three years of arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning anything new in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it kept me on the books till sixty-six, I'd sit through it. Not because I want to. I'd do it for the pension, the same way I did my climbing tickets every two years.

S3.say: I'd say the government has to get ahead of it and that with five years there's no excuse. I'd push the union branch hard for a deal while the company still needs us.
S3.think: Five years takes me to sixty-three, which is close enough that I might hold on if the union wins something. A three-year gap is still a worry, but one I can almost picture.
S3.do: Starts saving about fifty a week from day one and joins the union working group for older members. Asks the company about a part-time standby role near the end, and would sit through retraining if it kept him on the books.
S3.feel: Still frightened, but with a bit more room to breathe.
S3.quote: It's the difference between a fault at midnight and a planned outage with a date on the letter.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years matter mainly because they give the union time to fight. He would learn something new, but only as a means to reach the pension. His trust is entirely in collective bargaining, drawing on a past win over shift patterns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for the government to do it right for once: retrain the young ones, protect the older ones, tax the companies that profit. I'd say it at the pub and at the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be sixty-eight. I'd be out by then, retired, pottering in the allotment. It's the young ones I'd worry for, Jake and my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to sixty-six like I planned. I'd push the union to get training for the younger ones while there's time. And I'd tell my son to get a trade a robot can't do, though God knows what that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm for me. But there's a sad bit, that the job I've done might just stop after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine, but your savings are thin. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would if we started now. Linda and I have talked about it before and never done it. Ten years of a bit each week would give us something, but I'd be lying if I said we'd stick to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jake about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn whatever the drones and robots need, because someone's got to fix them. And I'd tell him to join the union on day one, which he already has, I made sure of that.

S4.say: I'd say it's a chance for the government to do it right, retraining the young, protecting the older workers and taxing the companies that profit. I'd say that at the pub and at the branch.
S4.think: I'd be sixty-eight and retired by then, so my worry is for Jake and my son. My own risk is mostly that we still haven't saved.
S4.do: Keeps working to sixty-six as planned and pushes the union to win training for younger workers. Tells his son to find a trade robots can't easily do, and talks about saving a little each week.
S4.feel: Mostly calm for himself, with sadness that his trade may end after him.
S4.quote: There's a sad bit, that the job I've done might just stop after me.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Adam's own path is safe on paper, so his concern turns to the young. He admits he and Linda have talked about saving for years and never stuck to it. He's proud of having signed the apprentice up to the union.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is a bridge to the pension, something that pays older workers from when the job goes to when the pension starts. And the union having a seat at the table, not a letter after the decision.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. It won't be the lads on the trucks and it won't be the robots. It'll be six people in a meeting room who've never been up a pole in sleet, and that's what I'd want written down.

headlineQuote: It'll be six people in a meeting room who've never been up a pole in sleet, and that's what I'd want written down.
portrait: Adam Chen is a fifty-eight-year-old lineman at a small, lower-paid valley depot, thirty-one years on the tools, with about three weeks of savings and a wife who cooks at the local school. He refuses to use the job tablet and trades lessons with his apprentice in return for the screen work. He trusts the union and distrusts head office, and expects any change to be used as an excuse to cut. He is calm when AI fizzles, anxious about steady change, and panicked by AGI in two years because it would leave a six-year gap before his pension. With ten years' warning he expects to be retired and worries mostly for the young.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be sixty with no savings and six years before his pension pays properly.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge payment for older workers from when the job goes until the pension starts, and the union at the table before decisions are made.
